stem: Best guess: two founders transfer property to a new corporation for 100% of its stock. Generally, do they recognize gain?

choices.text: Yes, on all appreciation in the property
choices.explanation: §351 defers gain when transferors control the corporation.

choices.text: Only if the corporation is an S corporation
choices.explanation: §351 applies to C and S corporations.

choices.text: No, if they get only stock and have control
choices.explanation: Correct. §351: transferors in 80% control, receiving only stock, recognize no gain.
Corporations don't recognize gain on issuing stock.

explanation: §351: transferors in 80% control, receiving only stock, recognize no gain.

stem: A transfers land (basis $30,000; FMV $100,000) subject to a $45,000 mortgage to a corporation in a §351 exchange for stock only. What gain does A recognize?

choices.explanation: Only the excess over basis is gain.
Only the excess liability is taxed.

explanation: §357(c): gain equal to liabilities in excess of the total basis of property transferred.

stem: A father owns 50% and his son 50% of a corporation. The corporation redeems half of the father's shares. Is it substantially disproportionate?

choices.text: Yes, because the father drops to 33%
Yes, because any redemption is an exchange
No; with attribution he owns 100% before and after
choices.explanation: Correct. §318 family attribution: the father is treated as owning his son's shares, so his ownership stays at 100%.

choices.text: No, because redemptions are always dividends

explanation: §318 family attribution: the father is treated as owning his son's shares, so his ownership stays at 100%.

stem: A contributes property (FMV $80,000) and B contributes services (value $20,000) to a new corporation for 80% and 20% of its stock. Does A's transfer qualify under §351?

choices.text: Yes, and B also defers income
choices.explanation: B has ordinary income for services.
B isn't a transferor, but A alone has 80%.

choices.text: No — services disqualify the whole transaction
Yes — A owns 80% after the transfer
choices.explanation: Correct. A, the property transferor, owns 80% immediately after; B recognizes $20,000 of ordinary income.

explanation: A, the property transferor, owns 80% immediately after; B recognizes $20,000 of ordinary income.

stem: In a §351 exchange, C transfers property (basis $50,000; FMV $90,000) for stock worth $70,000 and $20,000 cash. What is C's recognized gain and stock basis?
A married couple filing jointly sells §1244 stock at a $140,000 loss. How is the loss treated?

choices.explanation: Correct. §1244: up to $100,000 ordinary for joint filers; excess is capital.

choices.text: $3,000 capital loss deduction only, the rest carried

explanation: §1244: up to $100,000 ordinary for joint filers; excess is capital.

stem: A redemption fails every exchange test. The corporation has ample E&P. How is it treated?

choices.text: Capital gain after recovering the shares' basis
A dividend to the extent of E&P; basis shifts
choices.explanation: Correct. §302(d) and §301: a nonqualifying redemption is a §301 distribution.

choices.text: Tax-free as a return of capital

explanation: §302(d) and §301: a nonqualifying redemption is a §301 distribution.

stem: A corporation completely liquidates, distributing land (basis $200,000; FMV $500,000) to its sole shareholder, whose stock basis is $100,000. What gains are recognized?

choices.explanation: Correct. Corporation: 500,000 − 200,000; shareholder: 500,000 − 100,000 (before reduction for any corporate tax paid).

choices.text: Neither party, because liquidations are tax-free

explanation: Corporation: 500,000 − 200,000; shareholder: 500,000 − 100,000 (before reduction for any corporate tax paid).

stem: Parent owns 85% of Sub's stock (vote and value) and liquidates Sub. What is the parent's result?

choices.text: Capital gain equal to the FMV received minus stock basis
No gain or loss; carryover basis in Sub's assets
choices.explanation: Correct. §332 and §334(b): no gain or loss; carryover basis and attributes.

explanation: §332 and §334(b): no gain or loss; carryover basis and attributes.

stem: Which planning step helps a shareholder qualify a redemption as a complete termination despite family attribution?

choices.text: Waiving family attribution, with no interest for 10 years
choices.explanation: Correct. §302(c)(2): family attribution waiver for complete terminations.

choices.text: Having the corporation redeem a small portion of shares
Staying on as an officer of the corporation
Selling some of her shares to her son first

explanation: §302(c)(2): family attribution waiver for complete terminations.

stem: A shareholder wants to transfer property with a built-in loss (basis $100,000; FMV $60,000) to her corporation under §351. Absent an election, what is the corporation's basis in the property?

choices.explanation: Correct. §362(e)(2): net built-in loss property takes an FMV basis unless the shareholder elects to reduce her stock basis instead.
Basis carries over, limited to FMV.

explanation: §362(e)(2): net built-in loss property takes an FMV basis unless the shareholder elects to reduce her stock basis instead.

stem: A corporation distributes loss property (basis $80,000; FMV $50,000) to a 10% unrelated shareholder in complete liquidation. The property wasn't recently contributed. Can the corporation recognize the loss?

choices.explanation: Correct. §336(d) limits losses on distributions to related persons (>50%) or of recently contributed built-in loss property; neither applies.

choices.text: No — losses are never allowed in liquidations

explanation: §336(d) limits losses on distributions to related persons (>50%) or of recently contributed built-in loss property; neither applies.

stem: A shareholder needs $200,000 from her C corporation. Her stock basis is $300,000 and she will remain a 30% owner of an otherwise unrelated group after a redemption (was 45%). Which approach likely costs the least tax?

choices.explanation: Fully taxable with no basis recovery.
Correct. 30% < 50% and < 36% (80% × 45%) → exchange treatment: capital gain only on the excess over the redeemed shares' basis.

choices.text: It makes no difference in total tax
choices.explanation: Basis recovery reduces the taxable amount.

explanation: 30% < 50% and < 36% (80% × 45%) → exchange treatment: capital gain only on the excess over the redeemed shares' basis.

stem: A business has a $200,000 built-in gain on its assets (fair value $500,000). As a C corporation it would sell the assets, pay 21% tax and distribute the cash to the owner, whose stock basis is $100,000. As an S corporation with no built-in gains tax, the gain would pass through and the owner's basis would rise to match the cash. At a 20% owner rate, how much tax does the S corporation structure save?

choices.explanation: That is only the corporate-level tax.
That is the total C corporation tax, not the difference.
This compares the shareholder-level taxes only (71,600 − 40,000).

explanation: Liquidating a C corporation taxes the gain twice (§§336 and 331); an S corporation taxes it once.

stem: A C corporation made a $150,000 interest-free demand loan to its sole shareholder for personal use, outstanding all year. The blended annual rate is 5%. Neither party reported anything. What correction is needed?

choices.text: None — the de minimis exception applies to the loan
choices.explanation: The exception covers only loans of 10,000 or less.
Correct. Under §7872 the foregone interest is treated as a dividend paid to the shareholder and interest paid back to the corporation.
A loan to a shareholder gives rise to a dividend, not compensation.
Interest on a personal-use loan is nondeductible personal interest.

explanation: Below-market corporation–shareholder loans produce a deemed dividend to the shareholder and interest income to the corporation.

stem: A C corporation with ample E&P distributes land (basis $40,000, fair value $100,000) to its sole shareholder. What are the corporation's gain and the shareholder's dividend?

choices.explanation: Appreciated property triggers corporate gain, and the dividend is measured at fair value.
The shareholder's dividend is the property's fair value, not its basis.
Correct. §311(b) treats the distribution as a sale (gain 60,000); the shareholder has a dividend equal to fair value.
A corporation recognizes gain on distributing appreciated property.

explanation: C corporation property distributions: corporate gain on appreciation, dividend at fair value, shareholder basis at fair value.

stem: An S corporation (never a C corporation) distributes equipment with a basis of $10,000 and a fair value of $25,000 to its sole shareholder, whose stock basis before the distribution is $50,000. What is the shareholder's stock basis afterward (ignoring other items)?

choices.explanation: This reduces basis by fair value but omits the passed-through gain.
This subtracts the fair value twice.
This reduces basis by the corporation's basis in the equipment instead of fair value.
Correct. The §311(b) gain of 15,000 passes through (basis 65,000); the distribution then reduces basis by fair value (25,000), leaving 50,000.

explanation: S corporation property distributions: the gain passes through and increases basis; the distribution reduces basis by fair value.

stem: A transfers property for 70% of a new corporation's stock; B receives 30% solely for services. Does A get §351 nonrecognition?

choices.explanation: B's stock for services doesn't count.
Correct. B isn't a property transferor.

choices.text: Yes, if B pays tax on the stock

explanation: Stock received solely for services isn't counted toward the 80% control test; A alone holds 70%.

stem: A father's shares are all redeemed, but his son still owns shares. How can the father get exchange treatment?

choices.text: Gift his shares to the son first

choices.explanation: Correct. With no interest except as creditor for 10 years.

explanation: §302(c)(2): family attribution may be waived for a complete termination if the shareholder keeps no interest (other than as creditor) for 10 years.

stem: An estate redeems stock to pay death taxes and funeral expenses. Which provision can give exchange treatment?

choices.explanation: That's for small business stock losses.
Correct. Redemptions to pay death taxes.

explanation: §303 treats qualifying redemptions to pay estate taxes and expenses as exchanges.

stem: A corporation closes one of two active business lines (each run 5+ years) and distributes the proceeds to individual shareholders pro rata. How are they taxed?

choices.explanation: Correct. Exchange treatment for noncorporate holders.

choices.text: As a dividend, being pro rata

explanation: §302(b)(4): a partial liquidation from contraction of a business gives noncorporate shareholders exchange treatment.

stem: In a complete liquidation, what is a shareholder's basis in property received?

choices.explanation: Correct. Gain was recognized on the exchange.
That isn't what the rule says.

explanation: In a taxable liquidation, the shareholder takes a fair market value basis in distributed property.

stem: In a §351 exchange, a shareholder transfers a capital asset held 3 years. What is the holding period of the stock received?

choices.text: It starts on the exchange date

explanation: Stock received for capital or §1231 assets in a §351 exchange includes the holding period of those assets.

stem: In a §351 exchange, a shareholder transfers asset A (basis $20,000; FMV $60,000) and asset B (basis $80,000; FMV $40,000) for stock worth $90,000 and $10,000 cash. What gain is recognized?

choices.explanation: Boot is allocated among the assets.
Correct. Boot is allocated by FMV: A gets $6,000; B's loss isn't recognized.

explanation: Boot is allocated to each asset in proportion to FMV; each asset's gain is the lesser of its realized gain or allocated boot.

stem: An estate redeems stock to pay estate taxes of $300,000 and funeral and administration expenses of $100,000. It redeems $500,000 of stock. How much qualifies for §303 exchange treatment?

choices.explanation: Funeral and administration expenses count too.
Correct. §303 is limited to death taxes plus funeral and administration expenses.

explanation: §303 treats redemptions up to death taxes and funeral/administration expenses as exchanges.

stem: A parent owns 70% of a subsidiary, which liquidates and distributes appreciated assets. What is the tax effect?
explanation: Without 80% control, the liquidation is taxable under §336 and §331.

stem: What control test must transferors meet under §351?
explanation: Transferors must own at least 80% of voting power and 80% of each other class of stock.

stem: What ownership must a parent have for a tax-free §332 liquidation of a subsidiary?
explanation: §332 requires the parent to own at least 80% of the subsidiary's vote and value.

stem: What does the substantially disproportionate redemption test require?
explanation: After the redemption, the shareholder must hold less than 50% of voting power and less than 80% of the prior percentage.

stem: Land (basis $60,000, FMV $100,000) is transferred for $90,000 of stock and $10,000 cash in a §351 exchange. What is the gain and stock basis?

choices.explanation: Boot is taxed in this case.

explanation: Stock basis equals property basis plus gain less boot.

stem: Property with a $50,000 basis and $200,000 FMV, subject to an $80,000 liability, is transferred in a §351 exchange. What gain is recognized?
explanation: Liabilities in excess of basis cause gain under §357(c).

stem: In the §351 exchange above (land basis $60,000, $10,000 of gain recognized), what is the corporation's basis in the land?

choices.explanation: Add the gain in this case.

explanation: The corporation takes the transferor's basis plus any gain recognized.

stem: A founder receives 10% of a new corporation's stock, worth $50,000, for services. What results?
explanation: Stock received for services is compensation income.

stem: A transfers property for 70% of a new corporation's stock, and B receives 30% for services only. Does §351 apply to A?

choices.explanation: Correct. B isn't a property transferor.

explanation: Stock for services doesn't count toward the 80% control test.

stem: A C corporation liquidates, distributing land (FMV $500,000, basis $200,000) to its sole shareholder (stock basis $100,000). What gain arises?
explanation: §336 taxes the corporation on distributed appreciation; §331 taxes the shareholder on the excess over stock basis.

stem: An 85%-owned subsidiary liquidates into its parent. What gain does the parent recognize, and what basis does it take?
explanation: In a §332 liquidation, the parent recognizes no gain and takes the subsidiary's basis.

stem: In a §332 liquidation, the subsidiary distributes appreciated property to its 15% minority shareholder. What results?

choices.explanation: Correct. On distributions to minority holders.

explanation: A subsidiary recognizes gain (not loss) on distributions to minority shareholders.

stem: A shareholder owns 60 of 100 shares. The corporation redeems 30 of her shares. Is the redemption substantially disproportionate?
explanation: 30/70 = 42.9%, below 50% and below 80% of 60%.

stem: A mother and son each own 50 of 100 shares. The mother's 50 shares are redeemed. Without a waiver, is it a complete termination?
explanation: §318 family attribution treats her as owning her son's shares unless she waives it.

stem: A corporation with $100,000 of E&P redeems $40,000 of a shareholder's stock, and no §302 test is met. How is it treated?
explanation: Redemptions failing §302(b) tests are distributions, taxed as dividends to the extent of E&P.

stem: In a merger, a target shareholder (basis $100,000) receives acquirer stock worth $150,000 and $100,000 cash. What gain is recognized?

choices.explanation: Correct. Gain is recognized up to the boot.
Boot is taxed in this case.

explanation: In a reorganization, realized gain is recognized to the extent of boot received.

stem: In a Type B reorganization, what may the acquirer use to obtain 80% control of the target?
explanation: A Type B reorganization requires solely voting stock for target stock, achieving 80% control.

stem: A founder plans to contribute built-in loss property for stock under §351. What limits loss duplication?

choices.explanation: Correct. Corporate basis is limited to FMV.

explanation: §362(e)(2) limits the corporation's aggregate basis in net built-in loss property to FMV.

stem: A transferor's liabilities exceed the basis of the property contributed. How can she avoid §357(c) gain?
explanation: Adding cash or other basis property raises total basis above the liabilities assumed.

stem: A buyer wants a basis step-up in a C corporation's assets, but the seller prefers a stock sale. What's the tension?

choices.explanation: Correct. The seller pays two levels.

choices.text: A stock sale gives a step-up

explanation: Asset sales give buyers a step-up but create corporate and shareholder tax for C corporation sellers.

stem: A buyer acquires all stock of an S corporation and wants an asset basis step-up. What can help?

choices.explanation: Correct. Stock sale treated as asset sale.

explanation: A joint §338(h)(10) or §336(e) election treats the stock purchase as an asset purchase.

stem: A retiring shareholder's shares are redeemed, and her children keep theirs. How can she get exchange treatment?
explanation: A complete termination with a family attribution waiver requires no interest (other than as a creditor) for 10 years.

stem: A transferor contributes built-in loss property and wants the corporation to keep the full basis. What election is available?
explanation: The transferor and corporation may elect to reduce stock basis instead of the property's basis.
